source.title: Do We Need Zero Training Loss After Achieving Zero Training Error?
source.authors: Takashi Ishida; Ikko Yamane; Tomoya Sakai; Gang Niu; Masashi Sugiyama

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses double descent and reports epoch-wise double descent in test loss as a byproduct of flooding. It does not test the claim versions as stated: the reported outcome is test loss rather than test error, and the curve is produced while deliberately applying flooding.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-loss learning curves under flooding. These relate to the claim's subject but do not measure test error or establish naturally occurring epoch-wise double descent. Its test-accuracy comparisons for flooding versus other regularizers do not sweep model size, epochs, or sample size as the claim versions require.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes flooding, a training-loss floor regularizer. It deliberately alters training and reports, as a byproduct, an epoch-wise double-descent shape in test loss, not test error. It does not sweep model size or sample size, does not measure epoch-wise test error double descent under standard training, and does not test noise or regularization dependence of a double-descent peak. Double descent appears only as background (Sec. 2.2) and as a byproduct under the authors' own intervention. The authors say linking it to prior double descent is out of scope.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude flooding improves test accuracy across synthetic and benchmark datasets and reduces risk-estimator MSE under conditions. As a byproduct it produces a double-descent test-loss curve, whose relation to prior double descent is left to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a flooding modification to the training objective and plots test loss over epochs; it does not reproduce the cited size, epoch-error, or sample-size measurements of the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The plotted outcomes vary across dataset and model setups and across flood levels. The experiments also compare settings with and without early stopping, batch normalization, data augmentation, and learning-rate decay.

fits_no_version.finding: With flooding, test loss over epochs shows a fall-rise-fall shape in most benchmark setups. The authors say this was not previously observed for test loss. Baselines without flooding show test loss rising without a second descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A training-loss floor (flooding) induces epoch-wise double descent in test loss of image classifiers.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: The double-descent curves are shown in figures without exact numerical values. The paper reports the curve for test loss, not test error, and the reported double descent is produced under flooding.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant result rows left out. Repeated displays of the same learning curves in Figure 6 and Appendix Figures 7–8 were not added where they duplicate results already represented.

untested.parts: No sweep over model size; only fixed architectures (MLP, ResNet-18, ResNet-44).
Learning curves are test loss, not test error, and the second descent appears only under flooding; standard-training epoch-wise test-error curves are not analysed.
No capacity sweep past interpolation in any model class.
No effective-complexity measure is related to peak location.
Label noise (1/5/10%) is varied only in synthetic accuracy experiments; it is not linked to a double-descent peak, peak splitting, or removal by tuned regularization.

record.verdict_notes: Rows are appropriately linked to 'none'. r1 is an aggregate author statement ('in most cases') read from Figure 2; r2-r11 are figure-only panels. The Fig. 3 finding that the validation-chosen flood level often keeps zero training error is cited by the authors as consistent with Belkin/Nakkiran. It is not a double-descent measurement and does not need a row.

versions.untested_parts: The paper plots test loss, not test error, over epochs; the double-descent behavior is reported under flooding.
No sweep over training sample size near an interpolation threshold.
No cross-model-class test of risk beyond an interpolation point.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested against peak locations.
The experiments vary label noise in synthetic data, but do not test whether it drives double-descent peaks, whether peaks split, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes them.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameters or test of whether that produces an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: benchmark datasets and models (aggregate; most cases)
rows.operation_detail: Train with the flooding objective and compare test-loss learning curves with training without flooding.

conditions.value: multiple flood levels; benchmark candidates from 0.00 to 0.10

rows.measure: test loss over epochs; whether the curve shows double descent
rows.value: lower test loss with a double descent curve in most cases
rows.note: The authors state this result at aggregate level; they do not identify which individual plots account for 'most cases'. This is test loss under flooding, not test error.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Train with flooding at a stated flood level and plot test loss over epochs against the no-flooding baseline.
rows.note: The paper identifies the plotted comparison and flood level, but gives no per-curve textual characterization of the double-descent shape.
